beats.say: Keep your finger here. The engineer needs the expiry of a legacy-token exception. When the migration summary folds over this passage, it keeps the usual rule. The engineer still has an October first job to schedule.
Look at the page tabs. One gives the overview, one gives the condition, and one gives the expiry. Which page would you reopen to decide whether the October job can use the old token?

Open page six. The exception expires on September thirtieth. October first comes a day later. A recursive language model can keep the complete manual outside its prompt, write code to inspect a passage, and send a bounded slice to a child model. Let’s follow the page number through the investigation.

title: A page that fits through the window

beats.say: The root model gets the question, the manual version, the page format and permission to read these eight pages. Its code runs in a read-eval-print loop, or REPL. The interpreter can keep variables between turns. The authoritative manual stays in a read-only snapshot, so changing a working variable leaves the original available.

Read page six. Copy its exact sentence and page pointer into the child request. The sentence uses thirty-four characters of our ninety-six-character slice allowance. Instructions and the pointer take space too. In deployment, tokenize the complete request and reserve output space before dispatch.

Which work belongs to a child? A plain call can extract the date from this sentence. A nested controller can use its own working variables to follow a reference and inspect another authorized span. Give either child the mission and the scope it needs. The parent receives response text. With sub-calls disabled, the root can still use the interpreter itself.

Start a fresh evidence record for two runs. Both use legacy tokens with audit logging on. Search the overview, authentication, version history and migration pages. None gives either required clause. A source can be available while the controller’s evidence record is still empty.

Page five supplies the condition. Keep its pointer. Now search for the word expires. Page six supplies the expiry. Put that date between the September twenty-ninth run and the October first run. Which one do both clauses cover?

The September run qualifies. The October run is late. Both jobs have logging on. The difference comes from the date on page six. A reader who has both pointers can check exactly why the decisions differ.

Try a fixed split-and-merge plan. Read the eight pages independently. Count a leaf when its page read finishes. Pages five and six contribute different pieces of the exception. At the bottom of the tree, both clauses are available.

Merge adjacent pairs into four reports. Merge those four into two. Join the last two reports at the root. Every merge consumes another request. Eight leaves and seven merges make fifteen. Each merge must fit its two inputs, instructions and reserved output.
Read this supplied root answer. The condition survived, but the expiry field is empty. Every page was visited. Which original page would you reopen to recover the missing field?

Follow the empty field back to page six. Read the date again and attach its pointer. The tree still cost fifteen requests. This separate source lookup repairs the evidence record. It also explains why you should keep complete clauses together when splitting a manual.

title: How small can the window get?

beats.say: A full binary tree turns two results into one at every merge. With sixteen leaves you need fifteen merges. Try a character-counted baseline on fifty-seven hundred source characters. A five-hundred-twelve-character window spends eighteen on instructions and reserves thirty-two for output. Four hundred sixty-two source characters fit in a leaf.

Halve each slice until it fits. Sixteen leaves yield thirty-one requests. Each digest is sixteen characters long. Now halve the window too. The new source allowance is two hundred six. It takes thirty-two leaves and sixty-three requests. These calls return fixed-size digests. Finishing them tells us the plumbing works. It tells us nothing about the date.

Now try a sixty-four-character window. The shortest merge needs two sixteen-character digests, their separator, its instruction and the output reserve. Together they need eighty-nine characters. Reject this configuration before the first call. A real model needs the same check in tokens with its actual merge inputs.

title: Can this candidate leave the loop?

beats.say: The interpreter prints a date and a page number. A printed line can be debugging text or an unfinished answer. The controller alternates inspection with bounded observations until the host recognizes a completion record or a limit ends the run.

Here is a candidate record. The content names the date and page six. The ready field contains the word false in quotation marks. Our wrapper requires an object, Boolean true, and nonempty text. Does this record pass?

The host rejects the string. Keep the content and change just the ready field to Boolean true. The host accepts the candidate for verification. Compare its date to page six before using it. Validate the type before a library converts it to text. Record a timeout, an exhausted step budget or a fallback as its own stop reason.

title: What fits in the next turn?

beats.say: Keep this raw return outside the prompt. It has four hundred nine characters. Cut a preview for history with a forty-character cap. The truncation marker needs fourteen places inside that cap. How many places are left for source text?

Twenty-six characters of source fit. Append the marker. Twenty such previews occupy eight hundred characters before any wrappers. The full returns would occupy eight thousand one hundred eighty. Both histories grow, even when each observation has a hard limit.

Before another turn, count the serialized instructions, code, metadata and history with the model’s tokenizer, then add the output reserve. If the next request exceeds the limit, stop with partial findings or compact and check again. Keep the mission and source pointers outside the compacted history. Save them with the stop reason and usage for recovery.

Try two fixed actions. Peek at the manual, then finish. In this fixture the second step stores a candidate. Replay the same actions with a smaller history allowance. The first observation now takes the serialized history over the limit. The host stops with a history-budget reason. It never reaches the finish step.

title: Who can spend the remaining balance?

beats.say: Give the whole tree one shared ledger with four calls and ten cost units. The root reserves one call and two units before dispatch. Send the request. It settles at one and a half units. The host releases the unused half. Each reservation must bound the actual charge.

Child A reserves three units and goes out. Its timer expires. The provider outcome is unknown. Keep the reservation charged. Child B also reserves three and goes out. It settles at two units. Reconcile that row before reading the balance.
Child C asks for two calls and four cost units. Read both remaining amounts. Can the host admit it while A is still unresolved?

Keep C queued. Only one call and three and a half units remain. C spends nothing. Use one atomic check and reservation across every worker, retry, compaction and fallback call. Otherwise several children can read the same available balance before any of them records a charge.

A depth cap still leaves room for repeated turns. Take a full tree with three children per controller and three edges to its leaves. One plus three plus nine gives thirteen internal controllers. Twenty-seven plain leaves make forty runs. Give each controller five requests and each leaf one. What allowance follows before retries?

Ninety-two requests. Multiply thirteen by five and add twenty-seven. Cap total children over each parent’s whole run. A per-batch cap lets the parent start another batch. Reserve each actual request against the shared allowance before it goes out.

Now schedule eleven independent equal-duration calls in three slots. Fill a wave before starting the next. The last wave has only two calls. That makes four ideal waves, down from eleven in a single slot. You still send eleven prompts and pay for their token work. Combining records into one prompt would change which records you retry together.

A private interpreter namespace gives a child its own variables. The executor enforces what that child may do. In this test fixture the declaration allows only a temporary file area, no guest secrets and no network access. The host also bounds memory and running time. Does accepting those settings establish that the boundary works?

Try a benign connectivity check. Suppose it reaches the test endpoint. The declaration passed, but the observed connection violates the policy. Pause this workload, repair the executor and verify the restriction. A second probe must confirm that the repaired boundary denies the connection before the workload can resume. Keep provider credentials behind a trusted proxy that enforces the parent’s permissions, input limits and shared budget.

Test a separate permission on our read-only manual. Read page six and keep the September date. Now ask to replace it with October fifteenth. The host denies the change. Read it again. The guest still sees September thirtieth. The network repair needs its own check.

title: Trace the reports to their sources

beats.say: The claim is that the legacy-token exception expires September thirtieth. One reader returns that date. Two more readers agree. Look at their page pointers. How many distinct source passages stand behind the three reports?

All three point to one page. Trace the lines back to the manual. A shared premise can travel down several branches. Ask a neutral question and send a reader to look for a record that could contradict the date.

A reader finds an October date in an export note. Check the scope. Billing exports are a different policy. An unknown ID also supplies no evidence. Count distinct, applicable sources. If the only applicable record gives the opposite date, the claim is contradicted.
Now open the bulletin for the same legacy-token exception. One applicable passage says September thirtieth. The other says October fifteenth. No precedence rule is supplied. Can we certify one date?

Leave the conflict unresolved. Keep both passages open. The three descendants of page six cannot outvote a second applicable source. An exact-field comparison exposes this disagreement. For free text, a reviewer still has to check what the passage actually establishes.

title: How much comparison work is there?

beats.say: Four records take four visits to scan. To compare every unordered pair, cross out the diagonal and keep one side of the square. Each remaining cell pairs two different records once. Double the record count. How many comparisons do eight records require?

Twenty-eight pairs. Each of eight records has seven partners. Divide by two because each pair has two ends. At ten thousand records the same calculation gives almost fifty million pairs. A single fact can still take a search to find. Pruning may reduce model calls if it preserves the comparisons that matter.

That workload matters when evaluating recursion. In the May twenty twenty-six study, GPT-five on OOLONG-Pairs gained F one from fifty-eight at depth one to seventy-six at depth three. On CodeQA, Qwen’s accuracy fell from sixty-six with the interpreter alone to fifty-six with plain sub-calls. Compare within the same model and task. Depth helps some workloads and adds work to others.

The study also trained an eight-billion-parameter root. The researchers took twenty-two hundred fifty candidate trajectories from seven hundred fifty tasks. Removing zero-score and single-turn runs left one thousand seventy-two. Selected root turns became training examples. The reported median gain across four tasks was twenty-eight point three percent relative. For scale, a quarter more than forty is fifty. A median across tasks cannot tell us one task’s gain.

Compare direct context, a controller with just an interpreter, and a recursive controller on the same held-out questions. These are invented results. Require exact fact recall of at least ninety percent, a ninety-fifth percentile cost at most thirty cents, and a ninety-fifth percentile latency at most twelve seconds. Which routes qualify?

The interpreter alone qualifies. Direct misses recall. Recursion exceeds both cost and latency. Among eligible routes choose the cheapest, breaking a cost tie by latency. Estimate percentiles over enough attempts and record uncertainty. Each live run still needs its own limits.
Keep those gates and try a fresh set of results. Direct and interpreter-only now both qualify. Which costs less?
Direct costs twenty-five cents. Interpreter-only costs twenty-seven. Direct wins. Keep the results fixed and lower the ceiling to twenty cents. Which route can still run?
Hold deployment. Even the cheapest route now exceeds the ceiling. In a real comparison include retrieval, and record actual tokens, failures, retries, latency and unsupported claims.

A backup restore uses approval logging. Its summary gives November first as the expiry. The cited page gives November fifteenth. Compare the condition and the date. How many required fields match? Can the summary clear the November twelfth restore?

One of two fields matches. The summary would refuse the restore. Copy the date from page two. Both fields now match. The twelfth falls before expiry. Leave that run on the schedule and add another on the sixteenth, also with approval logging. Which one does the source cover?

Only the twelfth qualifies. The sixteenth falls after expiry. If you delete the condition from the repaired summary, exact recall drops to one half. Adding an unsupported claim leaves that score unchanged, so check extra claims separately. Keep the source beside the decision. In the next lesson, several workers bring that evidence together.
